html:
The Choctaw are a Native American people of the Southeastern Woodlands, from what is now central and southern Mississippi and parts of Alabama and Louisiana. They speak a Western Muskogean language.

The Choctaw nation took shape in the 1600s, as people from older Mississippian chiefdoms regrouped after the epidemics and wars that followed de Soto's march of 1540. Their origin story centres on the mound of Nanih Waiya. They were farmers of maize, beans and squash, and among the strongest peoples of the region.

In the 1700s the Choctaw were the main allies of French Louisiana, while their northern neighbours the Chickasaw sided with the English. In 1830 the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek gave up their land, and under the Indian Removal Act they became the first large nation forced west, from 1831, on what became known as the Trail of Tears.

In 1847, still poor after removal, Choctaw people sent money to relieve the Irish famine. Choctaw soldiers served as code talkers in the First World War. Today they form the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and two smaller tribes in Mississippi and Louisiana.
